claims.text: Single-phase ZrB2 has strong Zr–B and B–B bonding.
Conventional consolidation of single-phase ZrB2 requires temperatures above approximately 2300 °C.
Lower-temperature-processed ZrB2 is susceptible to oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion.
Adding 5–10 atomic % Hf relative to Zr will produce a substitutional (Zr,Hf)B2 solid solution during sintering.
Hf addition will enable full or comparable densification at approximately 1700 °C.
The Hf-modified material will preserve or enhance mechanical strength relative to conventional high-temperature-processed ZrB2.
The Hf-modified material will have better oxidation resistance than conventional high-temperature-processed ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The Hf-modified material will have better liquid-metal corrosion durability than conventional high-temperature-processed ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
Hf modification will form a homogeneous solid solution with refined grain boundaries.
Hf has a similar ionic radius to Zr and a high melting point.
Hf substitutes for Zr in the ZrB2 lattice.
Substitutional Hf induces local lattice distortion that enhances diffusion during sintering.
Enhanced diffusion caused by Hf substitution promotes densification at lower temperatures.
Hf addition does not compromise the strong boride bonding network.
Hf modifies oxidation behavior so that a more protective and adherent oxide scale forms.
The modified oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The modified oxide scale improves liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
The beneficial effects are limited to approximately 5–10 atomic % Hf and may diminish above the Hf solubility limit.

contradictions.description: The stated comparison and falsification rule invoke conventional high-temperature-processed ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, but the experiment specifies only undoped and Hf-doped samples both sintered at 1700 °C. Thus, the designed control is not the high-temperature baseline required by the stated comparison.
